Empirical Research Plan – Minimum-Wage Differentials in Contiguous Border Counties, 1990-2006  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Two–way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DiD) implemented on matched county-pair × industry panels, complemented with an event-study specification to visualize pre-trends.  

Justification  
• The policy variation is generated by discrete changes in state minimum wages that differ across state borders. Neighbouring counties on opposite sides of a border provide a “local” counterfactual—geographically close, economically similar, but sometimes subject to different minimum wages.  
• Because the treatment status of a county can switch multiple times (when its state changes the minimum wage), a panel DiD with county-pair (or “border-pair”) fixed effects absorbs all time-invariant cross-border differences. Time fixed effects soak up nationwide shocks.  
• The event-study makes the parallel-trends assumption testable.  

Alternative strategies (pure cross-section RDD, IV on state politics, etc.) are less attractive here because (i) we possess a long panel with within-pair changes, and (ii) the running variable for a sharp RDD (distance to border) is constant over time, so RDD alone cannot separate time-varying shocks from policy effects.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
• Main: Treat_cst = 1 if the statutory minimum wage in county c’s state s at quarter t exceeds the minimum wage in its matched neighbouring state s′, 0 otherwise.  
   – Continuous version: ΔMW_cst = MW_s,t – MW_s′,t (winsorised at ±$2 for robustness).  
Control group  
• The “low-wage side” counties in each contiguous county pair at the same quarter.  
Treatment timing / event date  
• For every state-pair, the quarter in which MW_s,t first exceeds MW_s′,t (or changes by ≥$0.05) is event time 0. Event time k is k quarters relative to that change; counties on the low side get event time 0 but Treat = 0. A county can experience several events; we keep the first large divergence and censor subsequent ±6 quarter windows to avoid overlap.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel pre-trends within county pairs: in the absence of a minimum-wage change, employment in the treated and control counties would evolve similarly. Plausible because counties share a labour market, consumer base, and climate-related shocks.  
A2. No anticipation: firms and workers cannot perfectly foresee the change far in advance; any gradual adjustment begins within one or two quarters before implementation (we will drop 1 lead quarter in robustness).  
A3. Stable treatment intensity: once a higher minimum wage is implemented, the effective bite is governed by statute, not local exceptions. County-pair fixed effects absorb time-constant differential enforcement.  
A4. SUTVA / no cross-county spillovers large enough to overturn sign: although commuting flows exist, the main margin of adjustment (employment within establishments) is recorded where the firm is located; any spillovers bias the estimate toward zero.  
A5. Composition stability: the industry mix within counties does not change endogenously exactly at the policy date in ways unrelated to the wage change; including county-industry fixed effects mitigates this risk.  

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
T1. Differential local shocks (plant openings/closings, hurricanes) coinciding with policy changes.  
   – Mitigation: Add county-pair-specific linear trends; control for county-level unemployment insurance claims; re-estimate excluding quarters with major natural disasters.  
T2. Spillover hiring across the border (workers commute to lower-wage side).  
   – Mitigation: Present results for highly non-tradable industries (restaurants, retail) where cross-border production relocation is harder; measure commuting flows with LEHD to show they are small.  
T3. Policy endogeneity: states may raise the minimum wage when their labour market is booming.  
   – Mitigation: Border-pair FE nets out state-level time-invariant differences; national time fixed effects net out aggregate cycles. Additionally, include state-specific time trends and leading indicators (GDP growth) to show robustness.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Install/load packages
pkgs <- c("data.table", "fixest", "ggplot2")
lapply(pkgs, require, character.only = TRUE)

# 1. Load QCEW county–industry data
qcew <- fread("qcew_1990_2006.csv")   # assumes employment, wages, naics, county_fips, year, quarter

# 2. Load state minimum-wage history
mw   <- fread("state_minwage_1990_2006.csv")   # state, year, quarter, mw

# 3. Cross-walk of contiguous county pairs
pairs <- fread("contiguous_pairs.csv")         # county_fips, pair_id, side ('L' or 'H'), neighbor_state

# 4. Merge
dt <- merge(qcew, pairs, by = "county_fips")
dt <- merge(dt, mw,  by.x = c("state", "year", "quarter"),
                     by.y = c("state", "year", "quarter"),
                     suffixes = c("", "_own"))

# 5. Add neighbour’s min wage
dt <- merge(dt, mw,  by.x = c("neighbor_state", "year", "quarter"),
                     by.y = c("state", "year", "quarter"),
                     suffixes = c("", "_nbr"))

# 6. Construct treatment variables
dt[, diff_mw := mw - mw_nbr]
dt[, treat    := as.integer(diff_mw > 0)]          # high-side indicator
dt[, post_any := treat * !shift(treat, 1, type = "lag"), by = pair_id]  # first divergence

# 7. Main specification – FE: ln employment on statutory MW
dt[, l_employment := log(employment + 1)]

spec_main <- feols(l_employment ~ diff_mw |
                     pair_id + factor(year_quarter) + naics,
                   data = dt,
                   cluster = ~pair_id)
summary(spec_main)

# 8. Event-study leads/lags (-8 … +8 quarters)
dt[, rel_q := year_quarter - min(year_quarter[treat == 1]), by = pair_id]
event <- feols(l_employment ~ i(rel_q, ref = -1) |
                 pair_id + factor(year_quarter) + naics,
               data = dt[rel_q %between% c(-8,8)],
               cluster = ~pair_id)
iplot(event) + ggtitle("Event study: High vs. low minimum-wage sides")

# 9. Robustness: restrict to food & drinking places (722)
robust_food <- feols(l_employment ~ diff_mw |
                       pair_id + factor(year_quarter) + naics,
                     data = dt[substr(naics,1,3) == "722"],
                     cluster = ~pair_id)
summary(robust_food)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory is ambiguous: a perfectly competitive labour market predicts negative employment effects; monopsony or search frictions can yield zero or positive effects. Prior literature on border-county designs (Card & Krueger 1994; Dube et al. 2010) finds near-zero or small positives.  
Prior: Estimate β ≈ −0.02 to +0.01 elasticity. That is, a $1 increase (≈15 %) in the statutory minimum wage will change total county-industry employment by between −2 % and +1 %, with particularly small or zero effects in food & retail.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)  
C1: Display and test for parallel pre-trends via event study……………… 1  
C2: No anticipation or confounding contemporaneous shocks……………… 0.8 (some concern)  
C3: Stable unit treatment value (limited spillovers)………………………… 0.7  
C4: No differential sample composition/measurement error……………… 0.8  
C5: Correct standard errors and multiple treatment episodes handled… 1  

Overall internal validity ≈ 4.3 / 5 – strong but not perfect.
